# Little big: Sizing up the risk of mitigation deterrence from carbon removal

- Essay
- Open access
- Published: 27 June 2025

- Nils Markusson ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0002-7087-4905 1 

## Abstract

The risk that overall mitigation efforts will be deterred by the pursuit of carbon dioxide removal (CDR) is real. Some awareness about this risk among climate policy stakeholders appears to be widespread, but it is not clear that the risk is being taken very seriously. This essay identifies arguments for thinking that mitigation deterrence from CDR is not a big risk. These arguments revolve around removal being too small a thing to deter anything, and that other things are worse for deterring overall mitigation efforts. The essay presents counterarguments, facilitated by a shift of the perspective on technologies from being physical, stand-alone, apolitical things, to one where technologies also have discursive effects, are part of the wider phenomenon of technology in general, and are entangled with politics. The essay aims to strengthen the concern about mitigation deterrence from CDR, and so help justify efforts to pre-empt it.

## 1 Introduction

In the novel Little Big (Crowley 1981), the main character discovers an entry point to the realm of the Faeries in a seemingly normal house. Within the little house there lies an entire world. Similarly, carbon dioxide removal (CDR) technology may seem little, but is bigger on the inside, if we take into account the risk of mitigation deterrence.

The risk that overall mitigation efforts will be deterred by the pursuit of carbon dioxide removal is real. We know this through case studies (e.g. Brad and Schneider 2023; Palm et al. 2024; Olsson et al. 2024) and contextual knowledge mediated by social theory (Carton et al. 2023). And to the best of our knowledge the risk could be big. Grant et al. (2021) modelled that mitigation deterrence could be causing range from 0.3˚C overshoot of the 1.5˚C target if some mitigation in the 2020s is substituted with CDR which then fails to materialise. McLaren (2020) estimated that mitigation deterrence could cause an overshoot by as much as 1.5˚C, through a review of existing modelling literature, and included CDR substitution and failure, but also other mechanisms including rebound effects.

There is ongoing debate in the academic literature about mitigation deterrence, reviewed in Carton et al. (2023), with two main lines of disagreement. Firstly, about whether the deterrence that can be observed in modelled climate scenarios carries over into real-world practice. But the literature also clearly shows that integrated assessment models are performative, i.e. impact reality and make their results more likely to become real (see e.g. Beck and Oomen 2021). Secondly, some studies reduce mitigation deterrence to something individual actors deliberately do (moral hazard), and find no or limited empirical support for that through experimental and survey methods. But 1) people may act differently in practice than in experiments and when responding to surveys, and that deterrence is therefore better captured by case studies, and 2) deterrence is not necessarily the result of deliberate action, but also caused by social structures shaping behaviour so that deterrence becomes more likely, which is better captured by social theory and, again, contextualised case studies. The deterrence risk is real.

Awareness about mitigation deterrence risk among climate policy stakeholders appears to be widespread, and there are examples of support for counter-measures like separate targets for emissions reductions and carbon removals (Finnish Government 2023, He Pou A Rangi 2023), and serious discussion of the problem, especially in relation to the possible integration of CDR into emissions trading schemes (UK Government 2024; ESABCC 2025).

There are also ubiquitous reminders in the literature that CDR does not obviate the need for emissions cuts, that we need to do both removal and emission reductions (von Rothkirch et al. 2024), or, better, that we need to prioritise emissions reductions (e.g. European Commission 2021). But many such statements tend towards superficiality and remain vague as to how to counter deterrence in concrete policy practice. One possible reason for the frequent superficiality and vagueness is that whilst there is awareness about the existence of deterrence risks, or at least that the issue can’t be avoided entirely, there is as yet no consensus about it being a serious risk. For some—fossil-dependent industry interests, say—this is most likely often a deliberate downplaying of the issue, but there could also be genuine reasons for not thinking mitigation deterrence is a big thing. This paper is mainly addressing those in the climate research and policy community, who care about the climate crisis but are not convinced that deterrence risk is a big thing to worry about.

This paper aims to discuss the arguments involved (beyond those covered in the review of the academic debate above). Such arguments are rarely spelt out, likely exactly because the deterrence risk is not taken so seriously. Therefore, I will here have to draw mainly on my experience and imagination, illustrated by only a few examples. I will posit two sets of arguments, revolving around removal being too small a thing to deter anything, and that other things are worse for deterring or obstructing overall mitigation efforts, respectively. The arguments are inter-related, but here set out separately for clarity.

## 2 It’s not big enough to deter much

### 2.1 CDR deployment is tiny and it’s hard to scale it up

The first argument is that the volume of CDR deployed today is little, and hard to scale up, and therefore can’t deter much emissions reduction. CDR stakeholders from academia, industry, civil society and government used this argument in workshops about mitigation deterrence from CDR (McLaren et al. 2023).

The first argument is correct insofar that the current volume of deployed removal is little. There is about 2 GtCO 2 /y, but this is mainly land-based methods that have been accounted for in climate accounting as mitigation for a long time already, and a volume that to date has grown slowly. Novel, engineered methods grow faster, but the current volume is a miniscule 0.0013 GtCO 2 /y (Smith et al. 2024). This should be compared to modelling results showing that on the order of 7–9 GtCO 2 /y is required by 2050 to reach net zero (Smith et al. 2024).

But, the argument misrepresents how mitigation deterrence works. It is not so much the physical volume of deployed CDR that matters, but rather the very expectation that CDR will be used in the future that has its own impact, especially in combination with lacking or vague specifications about feasible amounts (e.g. Brad et al. 2024). Without clarity about feasible volumes, at specific times in the future, there is a clear risk that actors—countries and companies—rely overmuch on future removals that may not materialise, to justify low near-term abatement ambitions (McLaren et al. 2023; Carton et al. 2023).

McLaren (2020) estimated that mitigation deterrence could place at least as much CO 2 reductions at risk as that removed by CDR. It is anyway hard to scale up CDR, and scaling it up twice as much to compensate for the deterrence risk is of course even harder. And scaling up that much may not be feasible anyway, given limits to how much removal can be delivered sustainably; Deprez et al. (2024) estimate limits of 5.1 GtCO 2 /y for nature-based CDR, and 1.3–2.38 GtCO 2 /y for BECCS, and direct air capture consumes large amounts of energy that could be used for other things and have their own environmental footprints. If we can’t do without CDR, then it is well worth trying to find ways to avoid deterrence from it.

### 2.2 It’s only a small piece of the climate policy puzzle

A second version of this argument is that even if it turns out to be possible to scale up CDR enough, it is still only little in the context of the emissions reductions that are also needed to reach net zero, and the large set of different climate policy options that need to be pursued to achieve those emissions reductions. In other words, there are many more pieces of the puzzle to worry about than CDR, and any deterrence effect from it.

This argument is true in part. The hoped for contribution of CDR to net zero of about 7-9GtCO 2 /y, can be compared to the current level of emissions of around 54 GtCO 2 (equiv.)/y including other greenhouse gases (Jones et al. 2024). Emissions reductions will have to make a far larger contribution than removals.

But, vagueness about the relative proportions of emissions reductions to removals is common in texts about removals. To take a few examples from among company and government websites, see Carbonfuture (2025) writing that “ It's essential to turn off the tap that's constantly adding more water, but even that won't work unless we also unplug the drain to let it all flow out. Therefore, large-scale carbon removal needs to be deployed in tandem with other mitigation methods”, and the Swiss Federal Office for the Environment stating that rapid emissions reductions “ remains the top priority” (2022). And, as mentioned above, without clarity about feasible volumes and timings, actors risk over-relying on removals, and rely too little on abatement. Even if other climate policy options contribute more, the deterrence risk from CDR can be substantial.

Shifting the gaze to the period after net zero, when CDR takes on the role of helping to deliver net negative emissions, and the contribution of removals is larger than further emissions reductions, would bring the importance of CDR into sharper focus. But vagueness about amounts and timings is still possible, and, since that period is farther into the future, probably even easier.

## 3 Other things are bigger problems for climate change policy

### 3.1 Other technologies deter too, and more

The second argument is that there are other things that undermine abatement efforts more than CDR, and that other technologies are worse deterrents.

Other prospective technologies may well carry similar deterrence risks. This has been shown for e.g. hydrogen (Szabo 2020), next-generation biofuels, and solar radiation management (Low and Boettcher 2020). And maybe those deterrence risks are bigger.

But, CDR hype contributes to a more general discourse of technology optimism that works to delay climate action (Lamb et al. 2020). And it is not clear how big the deterrence impacts of other individual technologies are. Until someone manages to quantify the relative deterrence impacts of a range of technologies, it is reasonable to worry about each individual one.

That said, there are reasons to think that CDR plays a special role, among other prospective climate technologies. Firstly, assuming equivalence between any two mitigation options is always problematic, as they most likely have different (positive and negative) side-effects. For CDR techniques involving geological sequestration (alongside fossil CCS) this is compounded by a risk of the sequestered CO 2 leaking and re-entering the atmosphere, and for biological sequestration the leakage risk is much higher. Any substitution of removals for emissions reductions, runs the extra risk of sequestration failure, making the deterrence impact worse. Secondly, the current master frame of climate policy is ‘net zero’, under which residual emissions will have to be compensated for by removals. This gives CDR a pivotal, mandatory role in climate policy until we reach net zero.
